entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Doukas dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Doukas dynasty (1059-1081 CE) governed one of the most catastrophic periods in Byzantine military history — the decades of the Battle of Manzikert (1071 CE), in which Seljuk Turkish forces captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes (who had married into the Doukas family), effectively opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement and permanently transforming the demographic and religious character of Asia Minor. The Doukas period is thus the pivot point from which the Byzantine Empire's eventual 1453 collapse becomes comprehensible.

Constantine X Doukas (r. 1059-1067) — an intellectual administrator who reduced military expenditure — left the empire militarily weak just as Seljuk pressure intensified. His widow Eudokia Makrembolitissa appointed Romanos IV Diogenes as co-emperor; his catastrophic defeat at Manzikert (August 26, 1071 CE) — the first capture of a Byzantine emperor in battle — broke the Anatolian defensive system. The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan immediately released Romanos in exchange for a ransom, but the Doukas faction refused to ransom him, deposed him, blinded him, and left him to die.

The Doukas period also saw the final political crisis leading to the First Crusade: the loss of Anatolia forced Emperor Alexios I Komnenos (who overthrew the Doukas in 1081) to appeal to Pope Urban II for Western military help in 1095 — the appeal that triggered the First Crusade. The Doukas dynasty thus links Manzikert to the Crusades: their military failures caused the imperial weakness that required Western Christian knights to fill.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Doukas dynasty — presiding over the Battle of Manzikert (1071), the most consequential Byzantine military defeat in history, which opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and set the trajectory toward the 1453 Ottoman conquest — governed the pivot period of Byzantine decline.
